questions.q: Which statement about concept drift is correct?
options: The inputs change but the rule stays the same
The rule from inputs to target changes
It can always be seen without labels
It is the same as seasonality
why: That is data drift.
Correct.
You need to see the error, so you need labels.
Seasonality is a pattern the model can learn.

questions.q: Training shares per bin: 40%, 60%. Recent shares: 60%, 40%. Compute PSI (use natural log).
Which signals need NO labels? (pick all)
options: Row count of today's input file
why: It only compares input distributions.
It looks at inputs only.
MAE needs the actual values.
A data quality check; no labels needed.

questions.q: Scenario: forecast error doubles, but PSI of all features is below 0.05. What is the best guess?
options: Concept drift or a changed business rule
why: Inputs did not drift, so it is not data drift.
Correct: the relation between inputs and target probably changed (price change, new policy, competitor).
Possible but less likely than a real change. Check the business first.
A doubled error is a real problem.

questions.q: Scenario: you have 180 features and PSI is checked daily with threshold 0.1. You get 15 alerts per day. What do you do?
options: Monitor only top features, tune thresholds from history, require several days in a row
why: Then you are blind.
Correct: fewer, better alerts are acted upon.
A threshold that never fires is useless.
This hides the problem and costs money.

questions.q: Bins for PSI must be built from:
options: The training (expected) data and then kept fixed
A new set of bins every day
why: Then both distributions look the same by design.
Correct: a fixed reference makes values comparable over time.
Changing bins breaks comparison over time.
Random bins give random results.
